n: Next, Ammon, a kingdom northeast of Moab. When the Assyrians deported Israel’s eastern tribes in the 700s BC, Ammon moved into Gad’s territory. God asks: doesn’t Israel have heirs? Why has Ammon’s king taken their land?

f.g: Descendants of Lot, like the Moabites; their capital was Rabbah (modern Amman, Jordan).
Hebrew malkam—probably “Milcom,” Ammon’s god (also in verse 3).

n: Battle alarms will sound in Rabbah, the Ammonite capital; it will become a ruin mound and its villages burned. Then Israel will reclaim its inheritance from those who took it.

f.g: Her surrounding villages.

n: Wail, Heshbon, for Ai is ruined; cry, women of Rabbah, put on sackcloth and run about inside the walls, for Milcom will go into exile with his priests and officials.

f.g: Not the Ai near Bethel, but an otherwise unknown Ammonite town; the name means “ruin.”
Walls or enclosures, perhaps sheepfold walls.

n: Why boast in your fertile valleys, faithless daughter, trusting your wealth and saying, “Who could ever attack me?”

f.g: Your valley flowing with abundance—or with blood.

n: God will bring terror on you from every side; you’ll be driven out headlong, with no one to gather the scattered refugees.
Yet afterward God will restore Ammon’s fortunes—another note of mercy for a hostile neighbor.

f.w: I will bring again the captivity of the children of Ammon

n: Now Edom, south of the Dead Sea, descended from Jacob’s brother Esau. Edom was famous for its wise men—has wisdom vanished from Teman? This section closely parallels the book of Obadiah.

f.g: A leading region or city of Edom; Job’s friend Eliphaz was a Temanite.

n: Flee, hide deep in caves, people of Dedan (Arabian traders in Edom), for God will bring Esau’s disaster on him.

f.g: Hide in deep places, caves.
An Arabian trading people whose caravans passed through Edom.

n: Grape pickers leave a few grapes behind; thieves take only what they want. But Edom’s destruction will be total.
God will strip Esau bare, exposing every hiding place; his children, relatives, and neighbors will be destroyed.

f.w: I have uncovered his secret places

n: Yet a tender note: “Leave your orphans with me—I will keep them alive; let your widows trust in me.” Even in judgment on a nation, God cares for its most vulnerable.

f.w: Leave thy fatherless children, I will preserve them alive

n: If even those who didn’t deserve to drink the cup of wrath (Judah, God’s own people) must drink, how could Edom go unpunished? It will surely drink.
God swears by himself: Bozrah, Edom’s fortress capital, will become a perpetual ruin and byword.

f.g: Edom’s capital, modern Buseirah in southern Jordan.

n: Jeremiah has heard a report from the Lord: a messenger has been sent among the nations calling them to rally and attack Edom.

f.w: I have heard a rumour from the LORD

f.g: Report, message.

n: God will make Edom small and despised among the nations.

f.w: I will make thee small among the heathen

n: Edom’s fearsome reputation and pride deceived it. Living in rocky cliffs (like the later city of Petra), it felt untouchable. But even if it nests as high as an eagle, God will bring it down.

f.g: Edom’s mountain strongholds; Hebrew sela‘, “rock,” was also an Edomite place name.
The terror you inspired in others.

n: Edom will be a ruin; passersby will be shocked and hiss at its wounds.
Like Sodom and Gomorrah, it will be overthrown and empty of people.

f.w: the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah

n: The invader will come like a lion from the Jordan’s thick jungle against a secure pasture, driving Edom’s people away in an instant. Who can stand against God? Who can summon him to court? What shepherd can resist him?

f.g: The dense thickets along the Jordan River, where lions lived.

f.w: who will appoint me the time?
f.g: Who can summon me to trial?

n: Hear God’s plan for Edom and Teman: even the smallest of the flock will be dragged away, and their pastures left desolate.

f.w: the least of the flock shall draw them out

n: The earth shakes at the crash of their fall; the cry is heard as far as the Red Sea.

f.g: Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds”; here probably the Gulf of Aqaba, on Edom’s southern edge.

n: The enemy will swoop like an eagle over Bozrah, and Edom’s warriors will be terrified like a woman in labor.
Next, Damascus and the Syrian cities of Hamath and Arpad. They are shamed by bad news and melt with fear, restless like a troubled sea.

f.g: The capital of Aram (Syria), north of Israel.
A city on the Orontes River in Syria.
A city in northern Syria.

n: Damascus grows weak and turns to flee; panic and anguish grip her like a woman in labor.

f.g: Grown weak.

n: “How can the famous city, the city of joy, be abandoned!” Damascus’s own people lament its fall.
Her young men will fall in the streets, and all her soldiers will be silenced that day.

f.w: her young men shall fall in her streets

n: God will set fire to Damascus’s walls and burn the palaces of Ben-hadad—a royal name used by several Syrian kings.

f.g: “Son of Hadad” (the storm god)—a title of several Aramean kings.

n: Next, the Arabian desert tribes of Kedar and the “kingdoms of Hazor.” Nebuchadnezzar attacked Arab tribes around 599/598 BC, as Babylonian chronicles record.

f.g: Nomadic Arab tribes descended from Ishmael, known for flocks and tents.
Not the Galilee city, but probably settled Arab villages (Hebrew hatserim).
Desert peoples east of Israel.

n: Their tents, flocks, tent curtains, goods, and camels will be taken, and people will shout, “Terror on every side!”

f.g: Tent cloths.

n: Flee far away and hide deep, people of Hazor, for Nebuchadnezzar has made plans against you.
Rise up and attack the carefree, prosperous nation that lives alone, without gates or bars—secure only because it seemed too remote to bother.
Their camels and herds will be plundered. God will scatter to every wind those who clip the corners of their hair, bringing disaster from every side.

f.w: them that are in the utmost corners
f.g: Those who trim the hair at their temples—a desert custom.

n: Hazor will become a lair for jackals, desolate forever, with no one living there.

f.g: Jackals.

n: Finally, Elam, a distant kingdom east of Babylon (in today’s southwest Iran). This message came early in Zedekiah’s reign (about 597 BC).

f.g: An ancient kingdom with its capital at Susa; later part of the Persian Empire.

n: God will break Elam’s bow—its famous archers were its greatest strength.
God will bring winds from all four directions and scatter Elam everywhere; its exiles will reach every nation.
Elam will be shattered before its enemies; God’s fierce anger and the sword will pursue them until they’re consumed.
God will set up his throne in Elam and remove its king and officials. He is sovereign even over the most distant lands.

f.w: I will set my throne in Elam

n: But in the latter days God will restore Elam’s fortunes. Fittingly, Elamites were among those who heard the gospel on the day of Pentecost.

f.w: I will bring again the captivity of Elam
